accordions.heading: What is HSV-2?
accordions.content:
HSV-2 is one of the two viruses that can cause genital herpes. The other is HSV-1. HSV-2 is associated with genital infection and is more likely to cause recurring outbreaks.

HSV-2 is passed on through skin-to-skin sexual contact. It can cause painful blisters or sores, but many people have no noticeable symptoms.

There is no cure for herpes, but outbreaks can be treated and managed with antiviral medicine.

accordions.heading: Is this for you?
accordions.content:
You don’t need to have symptoms to be concerned about HSV-2. Some people have no noticeable symptoms.

It may be worth testing if:

checklist: You’ve been sexually active and want to check your sexual health
A sexual partner has told you they have herpes or another STI
You’ve had possible symptoms in the past, such as blisters, sores or tingling around the genitals

benefits.text: Everything you need to test for genital herpes (HSV-2) at home:

how.heading: How does the test work?
how.intro:
The test looks for HSV-2 IgM antibodies using a small finger-prick blood sample. IgM antibodies can appear early after an HSV infection, but they can also appear again during a recurrence. This means the test cannot tell you when an infection was acquired or whether it is new.

Your result appears on the test cassette in around 15 minutes, with no sample to send to a laboratory.

steps.title: Prick your finger
steps.text: Wash your hands and clean your fingertip with an alcohol pad. Let it dry, then use the lancet to prick your finger and form a drop of blood.

steps.title: Add blood and diluent
steps.text: Use the pipette to collect your blood. Add 3 drops of blood to the sample well marked “S” on the test pad. Then add 1 drop of sample diluent to the same well.

steps.title: Read your result
steps.text: Leave the test pad flat while the test develops. Read your result between 15 and 30 minutes. Results read after 35 minutes are invalid.

windows.heading: When should I test?
windows.subheading: You can take this test if you think you’ve been exposed to HSV-2, whether or not you have symptoms. HSV-2 spreads through skin-to-skin sexual contact. Condoms reduce the risk, but herpes can still be passed on from skin that isn't covered by a condom. There isn't a reliable number of days or weeks after exposure when an HSV-2 IgM test becomes conclusive.

questions.question: When should I take an HSV-2 test?
questions.answer:
You may want advice about testing if you think you've been exposed to HSV-2 or a sexual partner has told you they have HSV-2.

If you have visible blisters or sores, a sexual health clinic can take a swab directly from the affected area.

questions.question: How soon after sex can I test for herpes?
questions.answer:
There isn't a reliable number of days after sex when an HSV-2 IgM test becomes conclusive. IgM antibodies can appear early after infection, but they can also appear during a recurrence, so the result cannot reliably tell you when an infection was acquired.

If you develop sores or blisters, contact a sexual health clinic as soon as possible. If you have no symptoms but are concerned about an exposure, a clinic can advise on other testing options.

questions.question: How reliable is this HSV-2 rapid test?
questions.answer:
In the manufacturer's clinical evaluation, 98.92% of IgM results matched those obtained using another commercially available HSV-2 test.

HSV IgM testing does have limitations. A positive result means HSV-2 IgM antibodies were detected, which can be consistent with HSV-2 infection. IgM can appear following an initial infection and may also be detected during a recurrence, so the result cannot reliably tell you when you acquired HSV-2 or whether the infection is new.

questions.question: What does a negative HSV-2 test result mean?
questions.answer: A negative result means HSV-2 IgM antibodies were not detected by the test. If you have symptoms or are concerned about a possible infection, speak to a sexual health clinic or GP.

questions.question: What if my result is positive?
questions.answer:
A positive result means HSV-2 IgM antibodies were detected in your blood, which can be consistent with exposure to HSV-2.

IgM can appear following an initial infection and may also be detected during a recurrence, so the result cannot tell you when you acquired HSV-2 or whether the infection is new.

If you have blisters or sores and want to confirm whether your symptoms are caused by herpes, visit a sexual health clinic while they are present so they can take a swab from the affected area.

If you have an outbreak, antiviral medicines can help treat your symptoms. If you have frequent outbreaks, treatment may also help reduce how often they occur. Recurrences vary from person to person — some people have repeated outbreaks, while others have few or none.

questions.question: What does an IgM result tell me?
questions.answer:
IgM is an antibody your immune system can produce in response to HSV-2. A positive result means HSV-2 IgM antibodies were detected, which can be consistent with exposure to HSV-2.

IgM can appear early after infection and may also appear again during a recurrence, so it cannot reliably tell you when the infection was acquired.

questions.question: I’ve had herpes before. Can I use this test?
questions.answer:
HSV IgM antibodies can sometimes appear again when the virus becomes active, so a positive result doesn't necessarily mean a new infection.

This test cannot confirm whether a current sore is caused by herpes. If you have sores or blisters, a sexual health clinic can take a swab to check what's causing them.

questions.question: Can this test tell me if I have genital herpes?
questions.answer:
This test detects HSV-2 IgM antibodies in your blood. A positive result means HSV-2 IgM antibodies were detected, which can be consistent with exposure to HSV-2.

Genital herpes can be caused by HSV-1 or HSV-2. If you have a current genital blister or sore and want to confirm whether it is herpes, a sexual health clinic can take a swab directly from the affected area.

questions.question: Can I take an HSV-2 test while pregnant?
questions.answer:
If you're pregnant and think you may have genital herpes, speak to your midwife, GP or sexual health clinic for advice.

This is particularly important if you develop new blisters or sores during pregnancy.
